title: Problem with your Florida condo board? How a complaint to the state works, step by step
seoTitle: How to File a Florida Condo Complaint With DBPR
description: What Florida's condo division can investigate, what it can't, how to file a complaint about your condo board, and what happens in the 90 days after.
dek: You asked for the records. You asked again. Nothing. Florida has a state office that takes complaints about condo associations, but it only handles certain problems, and it works in a certain order. Here is what it covers, how to file, and what to expect.
facebook: Asked your condo board for records and heard nothing back? The state takes complaints about condo boards, but only about certain things. Here is what it covers, how to file, and what happens in the first 90 days.
keywords: how to file a complaint against a condo association in Florida

Division of Florida Condominiums complaint process
condo board won't give me records Florida

body.text: Most condo questions get settled with a phone call or a letter to the board. Some don't. Maybe the records you asked for never came. Maybe an election didn't look right. Maybe nobody can tell you where the reserve money went.

Florida has a state office for that. It is the Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares and Mobile Homes, part of the Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR). This article explains what the division says it can look into, what it can't, how to file, and what happens after. It is a guide, not legal advice. For your own situation, the division, the condo ombudsman or a Florida attorney who handles condo law are the right people to ask.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: The Division: DBPR's Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares and Mobile Homes, the state office that oversees condo associations. Official records: the association's papers, such as minutes, contracts, budgets, bank statements and inspection reports. Ombudsman: a neutral state officer who helps owners and boards settle problems and points them to resources. Arbitration: a process where a neutral person hears both sides and decides the dispute, instead of a court. Chapter 718: the part of Florida law that covers condominiums.
What the state will look into
DBPR's condo website says its compliance team is the division's investigative arm. Its complaint page lists topics for condo associations controlled by the owners. They include:

items: Access to the association's official records.

Money matters: assessments, budgets, fines, financial reports, estoppel certificates, mixing association money with other money (commingling), misuse of funds, reserves and structural integrity reserve studies (SIRS, the study that sets how much to save for the main parts of the building).
A board that fails to answer an owner's written inquiry.

body.text: DBPR's frequently asked questions page also lists, as of July 1, 2025, meeting procedures, removing a board member, procedures for SIRS and milestone inspections (the structural inspection required for condo buildings three stories and taller), repairs a milestone inspection calls for, and board member education.
What it won't handle

Knowing the limits saves time. The complaint page says the division has no authority over homeowners' associations governed by Chapter 720. If you live in an HOA, not a condo, this office is not the place.

The division looks at whether the procedures were followed. It does not judge whether an engineer or architect did good work. DBPR's FAQ says complaints that a milestone inspection or SIRS was not done properly go to the Florida Board of Professional Engineers or the Board of Architecture and Interior Design. If DBPR receives evidence of a crime, its FAQ says it refers that to law enforcement.
Complaints about a licensed community association manager, a CAM, go through DBPR's general "file a complaint" system, which handles licensed professions.
How to file

The complaint page offers an online condominium complaint form and a PDF Condominium Complaint Form in English or Spanish. Each topic has its own checklist. The page says the form "should be accompanied by documentation that supports your allegation(s)." You can also file in person at one of the division's regional offices, or by mail to the Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares, and Mobile Homes, 2601 Blair Stone Road, Tallahassee, FL 32399-0791. The division's phone number on that page is 850-488-1122.
What happens after you file
DBPR's FAQ lays out the timeline:

items: Within 2 business days, the division confirms in writing that it got your complaint.
In about 10 to 15 days, intake staff check whether the issue is one the division can handle, whether it could be a violation, and whether you sent supporting papers.
At about 30 days, if the case moves ahead, an investigator contacts you about the allegations.
The division aims to finish within 90 days and sends written updates every 30 days.

body.text: If the division finds a problem, its lawyers decide whether there was a violation. For a first violation, the FAQ says the division usually educates the association and requires it to fix the problem. For repeat violations, it may impose civil penalties. You can check a complaint's status with DBPR's license verification search.
Other doors: the ombudsman and arbitration

A complaint is not the only option. DBPR describes the condo ombudsman as "a neutral liaison to help resolve disputes." The office helps with board operation and election concerns and runs the election monitor program. To ask for a state-appointed election monitor, owners file a petition signed by 15% of the total voting interests or six unit owners, whichever is greater. "Total voting interests" means all the votes in the association, not just the people who show up.

DBPR also offers non-binding arbitration for certain disputes, such as failing to hold elections or meetings properly, give notice, or allow records to be inspected. Arbitration cannot decide disputes over fees and assessments, title, warranties, tenant evictions or claims that the association failed to maintain the common areas. For condo disputes the filing fee is $50, and election disputes must be filed within 60 days after the results are announced. DBPR warns that if you lose, you may have to pay the other side's attorney's fees and costs. The law requires notice to the other side first, under section 718.1255(4)(b), so read DBPR's arbitration guide before filing.
What to do
If you are an owner:

items: Put your request to the board in writing first, keep a copy and note the date. A complaint goes further with paper behind it.
Check that your issue is on DBPR's list. If it is about an HOA, or the quality of an engineer's work, it belongs somewhere else.
Download the checklist for your topic and gather what it asks for before you file.
If you are not sure, call the ombudsman's office or the division first. A question is a good first step.

body.text: If you serve on the board:

items: Answer owners' written requests on time and keep a record of when and how you answered.
If the division contacts the association, call the association attorney and send the investigator what is asked for.
Use DBPR's free board education, including the four-hour board member certification course, to learn the rules before a complaint teaches them.

faq.q: How do I file a complaint against my condo association in Florida?
faq.a: Use the Condominium Complaint Form from DBPR's Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares and Mobile Homes, online or as a PDF, with documents that support your complaint. You can also file at a regional office or by mail to 2601 Blair Stone Road, Tallahassee, FL 32399-0791.

faq.q: What can DBPR do about my condo board?
faq.a: The division investigates topics such as records access, elections, budgets, reserves, SIRS procedures, conflicts of interest, insurance and unanswered written inquiries. For a first violation it usually educates the association and requires a fix; repeat violations can bring civil penalties.

faq.q: How long does a DBPR condo complaint take?
faq.a: DBPR says it confirms receipt within 2 business days, an investigator contacts you at about 30 days if the case moves forward, and it aims to finish within 90 days, with written updates every 30 days.

faq.q: Can I file a complaint with DBPR against my HOA?
faq.a: Not with the condo division. Its complaint page says it has no jurisdiction over Chapter 720 homeowners' association complaints, though its arbitration program does handle some HOA election and recall disputes.

faq.q: What does the Florida condo ombudsman do?
faq.a: DBPR describes the ombudsman as a neutral liaison who helps resolve disputes, helps with concerns about board operations and elections, and runs the election monitor program.
